abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical model and econometric framework to study when intermediate actions can serve as 'stepping stones' to eliminate harmful social norms. The authors derive conditions for stepping stones based on the relative size of social penalties and intrinsic utility benefits, then apply their approach to original data on female genital cutting in Somalia, finding that intermediate actions risk becoming new norms themselves.
keyFindings: The study develops intuitive theoretical conditions for when intermediate actions can function as stepping stones to norm elimination, contingent on the relative magnitudes of social penalties and intrinsic utility benefits.

Analysis of original data on female genital cutting in Somalia demonstrates the risk that intermediate actions may become entrenched as new norms rather than facilitating transitions away from harmful practices.
The econometric approach proposed enables empirical testing of whether specific intermediate actions qualify as effective stepping stones for norm change.
methodology: Theoretical model development with econometric testing framework applied to original data on female genital cutting practices in Somalia.
